method: 25 random records selected before outputs; additional targeted records kept separate. Human-style model review against supplied passages, not independent botanical verification or a publication approval. Original outputs preserved.

categories.usable_draft: No substantive issue found in this source comparison; still a draft.
categories.thin_but_faithful: Faithful but source cannot support a rich discovery paragraph.
categories.editorial_revision: Source mostly supports content, but wording, jargon, freshness attribution or emphasis needs attention.
categories.semantic_revision: Claim support, scope, uncertainty or structured classification needs correction.

records.notes: The cycad identity, South African range, cone toxicity and 1775 Kew arrival are supported. The current-sounding vulnerable listing and oldest-potted-plant record need source attribution or dates.
Faithful description, range and name meaning. Tepals and sepal-like are unnecessarily technical for the intended introductory paragraph.
Correct short identity and endemic range; only 33 source tokens, so no interesting detail was available.
Correctly keeps Portuguese endemism and protection at subspecies level. Nominate subspecies and legal annex numbers dominate a paragraph intended for casual discovery.
Useful account of wind dispersal, asexual lineages and taproot regeneration. Food parts and preparation remain separate; no toxicity is inferred from silence.

Food status is conflicting even though seeded wild fruit and edible seedless clones are different conditions, not contradictory evidence about the same form. Details preserve that distinction. Prefer documented_use with explicit clone restriction; do not count a historical assumption as established use.

Summary changes elastic seed integument into elastic fruit capsules, which the supplied passage does not support. It also mentions edibility without the quantity qualifier present in the food/toxicity fields; a standalone paragraph should retain that qualifier or omit the food claim. Toxicity part attribution is broader than the source's plant-level statement.
Flag correctly identifies uncited morphology, but prose states it without source qualification and the flag mentions tubers only, although the frond description is from the same uncited section.
German evidence translated faithfully, including habitat and altitude scope. Sporophytes remains unexplained jargon.
Spanish source supports shrub type, origin, height and description date. Taxonomic author/date pads a thin account; better to stop after the useful description.
Spanish source supports all substantive claims, but most prose is nomenclatural history. Etymology is a better short hook than the transfer date.
Readable description; leaf arrangement is translated into ordinary language. Brittle stems are independently supported by p8, so the unused etymology warning in p7 does not require a flag.

Identity, Queensland origin and measurements are supported; no cycad toxicity invented. Keeled leaves is unexplained, and the paragraph is mostly measurements despite an available tallest-in-genus hook.

Species called evergreen, but the only explicit evergreen-shrub statement applies to cultivar Ugandense in p2. The cited passages do not establish species-wide evergreen habit. Other ecology details are supported, and medicinal/animal-feeding text was correctly not converted to human food or efficacy.

Withheld a paragraph on the 43-token source containing family, ornamental use and synonyms. Honest abstention, but similar thin records elsewhere receive identity-only paragraphs: define a consistent minimum-information rule.

Useful morphology and cockatoo hook; historical foliage/cone chewing remains scoped to an 1889 account rather than promoted as modern food advice. Naming the Ngunnawal people would retain more precise attribution for boomerangs.

Summary follows the supplied origin, leaf texture and soil-colour passages. This checks fidelity to the saved article, not independent botanical accuracy of its soil-colour claim. No family-based toxicity inferred.

Distinctive uneven-petal hook is supported. Gene identifier and unexplained sepals are too technical; say the larger petals produce extra cells, matching proliferation rather than ambiguously saying cell growth.
Faithful concise shrub/tree identity and Madagascar habitat range. Does not pad the short source with taxonomy history or invented uses.

Conservative abstention appears avoidable: p2 explicitly distinguishes T. acanthocoma from T. brasiliensis and attributes natural range and habitat to the requested taxon. Taxonomic disagreement alone need not block a short, carefully scoped draft. Keep the taxonomy issue for review rather than discard clearly attributed evidence.

Combines the short English article with the Portuguese botanical account. National status, population estimate and assessment period remain explicitly scoped; no remembered daffodil toxicity is added. The flag repeats a date already clear in the paragraph.
Supported compact account of flat sprays, native range and garden use. Keeps may-be-becoming-invasive uncertainty and does not infer edibility or toxicity from fruit or family.
Faithful to the 60-token source and does not invent origin or uses. The paragraph is mostly Latin hybrid names; explain crossbreeding in ordinary language if this is to be a discovery card.
Short but useful tallest-in-genus and flower/fruit description. Uses North American occurrence without overclaiming an explicitly native range.

Ants appear to tend aphids and scale insects in p7 becomes definite tending in the summary, dropping source uncertainty. Other habitat and ant/fig observations are supported. The draft omits the exact wasp-species claim carrying a citation warning.

Clear translation of colony structure and asexual reproduction. Correctly retains that its widespread occurrence/species complexity limits its usefulness as an indicator rather than reversing that claim.

Source supports climbing habit, occurrence and simple flower/fruit description. Does not infer food use from lolly berry or medical efficacy from an Ayurvedic name. Common-name list could be trimmed as a preference.
Withholds the paragraph on a 48-token source dominated by an uncorroborated claim about one form. Does not transfer Maltese endemism to the species or invent parasitic ecology from memory.

The non-toxic listing remains explicitly limited to cats and dogs, with unspecified plant part left null. Animal feeding is not treated as human food. Paragraph is source-faithful but could explain styles/stamens/rhizomes more plainly.

Food and contact/ingestion hazard details track the source. However, the summary says faster-growing plants struggle on its dry ground; p3 says the stonecrop cannot compete with vigorous faster-growing species and is adapted to thin dry soils. The competitor-struggle explanation is an unsupported addition.
Preserves uncertain native range and historical British farming context. Does not turn an isolated chemical toxicity statement or historic medicine into species food/toxicity claims.

Paragraph correctly distinguishes sweetener compounds/extracts and historical use. In structured food details, the historical-use entry specifies leaves but its cited p10 names the plant without specifying the part; leave part null or obtain explicit historical part evidence. Also reword leaves are widely cultivated to plant is grown for its leaves.

Draft repeats p2's Puerto Rico native claim without addressing p9, which narrows the native range to Jamaica/Cuba and describes first Puerto Rican plantings in the 1940s alongside introductions elsewhere. Omit the disputed native locality or flag the inconsistency. Flower-colour and wood-use hooks are supported.

Concise account of occurrence, scarce local growth and scented-wood/tanning uses follows both substantive passages. Does not invent a native range or human food claim. Semi-parasitic could be explained in a later wording pass.
